Section 9.1 — Money: A Good Servant and a Cruel Master

Money is one of the great test cases of the heart, which is why our Lord spoke of it more than He spoke of heaven or hell. He knew that what a man does with his money tells the truth about what he worships, however carefully his lips may say otherwise. So let us begin with a distinction that will steer this whole unit: money is a good servant and a cruel master, and everything depends on which one it is allowed to become.

Scripture nowhere says that money is evil. It says something far more searching: "For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil, for which some have strayed from the faith in their greediness, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows" (1 Timothy 6:10). Mark the words carefully, for the verse is constantly misquoted. It is not money that is the root, but the love of it; not the thing in the hand, but the grip of the thing on the heart. A poor man can love money as idolatrously as a rich one. The question is never how much a man has, but whom he serves — and on this our Lord allowed no middle ground. "No one can serve two masters... You cannot serve God and mammon" (Matthew 6:24). Not should not. Cannot. Money makes a fine servant, sent out to feed families, support the work of the gospel, and relieve the poor; but the moment it climbs into the throne of the heart it becomes a god, and a jealous one, that will drive a man and never satisfy him.

Against that mastery Scripture sets the great weapon of contentment. "Now godliness with contentment is great gain... And having food and clothing, with these we shall be content" (1 Timothy 6:6–8). The contented man has broken money's power over him, for there is nothing it can promise that he is desperate to buy. This frees him to work honestly, to handle debt with sober care rather than presumption, to save with prudence and give with joy — to use money rather than be used by it. Teach your people contentment and you will have armed them against ten thousand financial follies. Leave them discontented, forever reaching for the next thing, and no amount of income will ever be enough.
Section 9.2 — The Prosperity Gospel: A Lie Refuted by Its Own Lord

We must now confront directly one of the most damaging distortions of our age, the so-called prosperity gospel — the teaching that God wills every faithful believer to be materially rich and physically well, and that poverty or sickness is the mark of weak faith. I will not be gentle with it, because it is not a harmless error; it preys on the desperate, enriches the preacher at the expense of the poor, and slanders the character of God. And the simplest refutation of it is the life of the One it claims to preach.

Consider Jesus of Nazareth. He owned no house: "Foxes have holes and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head" (Matthew 8:20). The whole of His earthly life was marked by material humility. He was laid at birth in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn (Luke 2:7). He rode into Jerusalem that final week on a borrowed colt that His disciples had to go and fetch. He ate the Last Supper in a borrowed upper room. He was buried in a borrowed tomb. And the one possession He had, the seamless robe upon His back, was stripped from Him and gambled away by soldiers as He died (John 19:23–24). If material wealth were the sure sign of the Father's favor, then the Son of God, the only perfectly faithful man who ever lived, was the most poorly rewarded of all. The prosperity gospel cannot survive ten minutes in the company of its own Lord.

And it is contradicted not only by His life but by His very first words from the mountain. "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 5:3); and in Luke's account, barer still, "Blessed are you poor, for yours is the kingdom of God" — with a matching woe the prosperity preacher never quotes: "woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation" (Luke 6:20, 24). Hear how completely that overturns the lie. The prosperity teacher pronounces blessing on the rich and suspicion on the poor; Jesus pronounces blessing on the poor and woe on the comfortable. He warned that it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom — easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle (Matthew 19:23–24). A message that promises God will make you wealthy is offering a blessing Christ never gave and ignoring a warning He plainly did. Do not preach it, and protect your people from those who do.
Section 9.3 — The Grace of Giving

If money is to be a servant, the noblest errand we can send it on is generosity, and the New Testament treats Christian giving not as a grim duty but as a grace — one more fruit of the Spirit at work in a freed heart. Its pattern and its power is the gospel itself: "For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, that you through His poverty might become rich" (2 Corinthians 8:9). There is the whole theology of giving in one verse. We give because we have first received from a Giver who gave away His very riches, His glory, His life, to make beggars like us rich. Christian generosity is simply the overflow of a heart that has grasped that grace; it gives because it has been given to.

From this Paul draws two principles every pastor must teach and guard. The first concerns the spirit of giving: "So let each one give as he purposes in his heart, not grudgingly or of necessity; for God loves a cheerful giver" (2 Corinthians 9:7). Giving is to be free, glad, and from the heart — and this rules out, sharply, the manipulative fundraising that has so often disgraced the church. There is no warrant anywhere in Scripture for pressure campaigns, guilt-driven appeals, or the emotional extortion of money from God's people, least of all from the poor. The pastor who works his congregation's feelings to open their wallets has corrupted a grace into a racket. Let the giving be cheerful, or do not seek it at all. The second principle is the promise that attends such giving: "God is able to make all grace abound toward you, that you, always having all sufficiency in all things, may have an abundance for every good work" (2 Corinthians 9:8). Note well what God promises the generous — not personal luxury, but sufficiency and the means for every good work. He resupplies the cheerful giver so the giver can keep on giving, not so he can hoard.

The tithe and the regular, disciplined support of the local church flow naturally from this. A congregation taught to give cheerfully will fund the work of God without ever being badgered, and the church's own finances must then be handled with the same transparency we required of the pastor in Unit 5 — open books, honest accounting, and not a whiff of the love of money about those who handle the Lord's.

Cross-Reference · Unit 5The transparency required in handling the church’s money, and the warning against using ministry for financial gain, were introduced in Section 5.4 and find their fuller theological grounding here.
Section 9.4 — Caring for the Poor — and the Pastor’s Own Table

The God of Scripture is, from beginning to end, the defender of the poor, and a church that does not care for the needy has not understood the God it claims to worship. This is not an optional add-on to the gospel; it is the gospel showing its hands and feet. James will not let us spiritualize it away: "If a brother or sister is naked and destitute of daily food, and one of you says to them, 'Depart in peace, be warmed and filled,' but you do not give them the things which are needed for the body, what does it profit?" (James 2:15–16). Faith that feeds the hungry only with kind words is, he says bluntly, dead. And our Lord pressed it further than we are comfortable with, identifying Himself with the needy so closely that what we do for them we do to Him: "Inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of these My brethren, you did it to Me" (Matthew 25:40). The hungry man at the door is, in a mystery, Christ at the door.

The prophets thundered this same truth long before. Amos heard God say something startling about the worship of His own people: "I hate, I despise your feast days... Take away from Me the noise of your songs" (Amos 5:21–23). How could God reject the very offerings He had commanded? Because the people bringing them were trampling the poor — bribing judges, cheating with dishonest scales, selling the needy for the price of a pair of sandals — and no offering covers for that. I learned the principle long before I could name it, from a friend I grew up with. On a Saturday night he would sometimes go out and do things he was not proud of, things involving alcohol and girls. But on Sunday he was faithful to put his tithe in the offering plate — almost as if the money were restitution, a way to settle the account. It does not work that way. God does not accept sacrifice in the place of obedience. What He asks, Micah said, is "to do justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God" (Micah 6:8) — and no check in the plate is a substitute for justice toward the people around us.

The negative warning is just as sharp, and our Lord gave it in the story of the rich man and Lazarus, the beggar at his gate (Luke 16). The rich man's sin was not that he actively harmed Lazarus; it was that he stepped over him day after day and did nothing, feasting in comfort while a fellow image-bearer starved at his doorstep. That is a sin a comfortable church commits constantly, and it damns. We help the poor, then, not with a careless sentimentality that merely throws money and feels good, but with the wise, personal, dignifying love that sees the person and not just the need — remembering always that the poor man bears the image of God as fully as we do, the principle we laid down in Unit 7.

And now a hard word that I will not soften, because it touches us who lead. It is a scandal and a contradiction for a pastor to live in a mansion while the members of his own congregation languish in poverty. Hear the principle plainly: if God blesses us with material resources, He gives them to us in order that we might share them. Wealth in a Christian's hand is a trust to be distributed, not a reward to be displayed. John puts the knife in: "whoever has this world's goods, and sees his brother in need, and shuts up his heart from him, how does the love of God abide in him?" (1 John 3:17). The pastor who grows fat on the offerings of poor people and parades his wealth before them has inverted the entire purpose of what God entrusted to him; he has become the rich man, and his flock is Lazarus at his gate. Let the shepherd's own standard of living be a sermon on contentment and generosity, not a monument to greed. He who handles the people's gifts must be, of all men, the freest from the love of money and the readiest to share.
Cross-Reference · Unit 7The principle that the poor man bears the image of God as fully as any other — the ground of his irreducible worth and our obligation to him — was established in Section 7.1.

sa.prompt: 21. Explain 'money is a good servant and a cruel master' and the role of contentment.
sa.model: Money is a good servant and a cruel master, and everything depends on which it is allowed to become. 1 Timothy 6:10 names not money but the love of money as a root of all kinds of evil, and Jesus says a man cannot serve both God and mammon. The great weapon Scripture sets against money's mastery is contentment: godliness with contentment is great gain. The contented man has broken money's power, for there is nothing it can promise that he is desperate to buy.

es_reference.prompt: 21. Explique «el dinero es un buen siervo y un amo cruel» y el papel del contentamiento.
es_reference.model: El dinero es un buen siervo y un amo cruel, y todo depende de cuál se le permita llegar a ser. 1 Timoteo 6:10 no llama raíz al dinero sino al amor al dinero, raíz de todos los males, y Jesús dice que nadie puede servir a la vez a Dios y a las riquezas. El arma que la Escritura opone al dominio del dinero es el contentamiento: la piedad con contentamiento es gran ganancia. El hombre contento ha quebrado el poder del dinero, porque no hay nada que este pueda prometerle que esté desesperado por comprar.

sa.prompt: 22. How does the life of Jesus refute the prosperity gospel?
sa.model: The prosperity gospel teaches that God wills every faithful believer to be materially rich and physically well. Its simplest refutation is the life of the One it claims to preach. Jesus had nowhere to lay His head, was born in a manger because there was no room in the inn, and lived out His ministry using a borrowed colt, a borrowed upper room, and a borrowed tomb—and as He died His one possession, the seamless robe, was gambled away by soldiers. If wealth were the sign of the Father's favor, the only perfectly faithful man who ever lived was the most poorly rewarded of all.

es_reference.prompt: 22. ¿Cómo refuta la vida de Jesús el evangelio de la prosperidad?
es_reference.model: El evangelio de la prosperidad enseña que Dios quiere que todo creyente fiel sea materialmente rico y físicamente sano. Su refutación más sencilla es la vida de Aquel que dice predicar. Jesús no tenía donde recostar la cabeza, nació en un pesebre porque no había lugar en el meson, y vivió Su ministerio usando un pollino prestado, un aposento alto prestado, y un sepulcro prestado — y al morir su única posesión, la túnica sin costura, fue jugada a los dados por los soldados. Si la riqueza fuera la señal del favor del Padre, el único hombre perfectamente fiel que jamás vivió fue el peor recompensado de todos.

sa.prompt: 23. How do Jesus' own words from the mountain overturn the prosperity lie?
sa.model: Jesus' first words from the mountain were 'Blessed are the poor in spirit,' and in Luke He blesses the poor and pronounces a woe on the rich, who have received their consolation. He warned that it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom—easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle. The prosperity teacher blesses the rich and suspects the poor; Jesus does the reverse. A message that promises wealth offers a blessing Christ never gave and ignores a warning He plainly did.

es_reference.prompt: 23. ¿Cómo desmienten la mentira de la prosperidad las propias palabras de Jesús desde el monte?
es_reference.model: Las primeras palabras de Jesús desde el monte fueron «Bienaventurados los pobres en espíritu», y en Lucas bendice a los pobres y pronuncia un ay sobre los ricos, que ya tienen su consuelo. Advirtió que es difícil que un rico entre en el reino — más fácil es que un camello pase por el ojo de una aguja. El maestro de la prosperidad bendice al rico y sospecha del pobre; Jesús hace lo contrario. Un mensaje que promete riqueza ofrece una bendición que Cristo nunca dio e ignora una advertencia que Él claramente dio.

sa.prompt: 24. How is Christian giving grounded in the gospel, and what spirit must mark it?
sa.model: The pattern and power of Christian giving is the gospel itself: though He was rich, for our sakes Christ became poor, that we through His poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). We give because we have first received from a Giver who gave away His riches. So giving is to be cheerful, free, and from the heart, not grudgingly or of necessity, for God loves a cheerful giver. This rules out sharply the manipulative fundraising and guilt-driven appeals that have disgraced the church.

es_reference.prompt: 24. ¿Cómo se funda la ofrenda cristiana en el evangelio, y qué espíritu debe marcarla?
es_reference.model: El modelo y la fuerza de la ofrenda cristiana es el evangelio mismo: siendo rico, por amor a nosotros Cristo se hizo pobre, para que nosotros con su pobreza fuésemos enriquecidos (2 Corintios 8:9). Damos porque primero hemos recibido de un Dador que repartió sus riquezas. Así la ofrenda ha de ser alegre, libre y de corazón, no con tristeza ni por necesidad, porque Dios ama al dador alegre. Esto descarta de raíz la recaudación manipuladora y los llamados que mueven a culpa que han deshonrado a la iglesia.

sa.prompt: 25. What does God promise the generous giver, and what does He not promise?
sa.model: 2 Corinthians 9:8 promises that God is able to make all grace abound toward the giver, so that having all sufficiency he may abound for every good work. Note what God promises—not personal luxury, but sufficiency and the means for every good work. He resupplies the cheerful giver so the giver can keep on giving, not so he can hoard. The promise funds generosity; it does not bankroll greed.

es_reference.prompt: 25. ¿Qué promete Dios al dador generoso, y qué no le promete?
es_reference.model: 2 Corintios 9:8 promete que Dios es poderoso para hacer que abunde toda gracia hacia el dador, de modo que, teniendo en todo lo suficiente, abunde para toda buena obra. Nótese lo que Dios promete: no lujo personal, sino suficiencia y los medios para toda buena obra. Él reabastece al dador alegre para que el dador siga dando, no para que acumule. La promesa costea la generosidad; no financia la avaricia.

sa.prompt: 26. How does the unit ground the church's duty to care for the poor?
sa.model: Caring for the needy is not an optional add-on to the gospel but the gospel showing its hands and feet. James 2:15-16 calls faith that feeds the hungry only with kind words dead, and Matthew 25:40 teaches that what we do for the least of these we do to Christ Himself. The negative warning is the rich man who stepped over Lazarus and did nothing—a sin a comfortable church commits constantly. We help the poor with wise, dignifying love that sees the person, not just the need.

es_reference.prompt: 26. ¿Cómo funda la unidad el deber de la iglesia de cuidar a los pobres?
es_reference.model: Cuidar al necesitado no es un añadido opcional al evangelio, sino el evangelio mostrando sus manos y sus pies. Santiago 2:15-16 llama muerta a la fe que alimenta al hambriento solo con buenas palabras, y Mateo 25:40 enseña que lo que hacemos por uno de los más pequeños lo hacemos a Cristo mismo. La advertencia negativa es el rico que pasaba por encima de Lázaro y no hacía nada — pecado que una iglesia cómoda comete constantemente. Ayudamos al pobre con amor sabio y digno que ve a la persona, no solo la necesidad.

sa.prompt: 27. State the governing principle on wealth and apply it to the pastor's own standard of living.
sa.model: The governing principle is that wealth in a Christian's hand is a trust to be distributed, not a reward to be displayed; if God blesses us with resources, He gives them that we might share them. It is a scandal for a pastor to live in a mansion while his congregation languishes in poverty—he has inverted the purpose of what God entrusted to him and become the rich man with his flock as Lazarus at the gate. 1 John 3:17 asks how the love of God abides in one who shuts his heart from a brother in need. Let the shepherd's own standard of living preach contentment and generosity.

es_reference.prompt: 27. Enuncie el principio rector sobre la riqueza y aplíquelo al propio nivel de vida del pastor.
es_reference.model: El principio rector es que la riqueza en la mano del cristiano es un fideicomiso para distribuir, no un premio para exhibir; si Dios nos bendice con recursos, nos los da para que los compartamos. Es un escándalo que un pastor viva en una mansión mientras su congregación languidece en la pobreza — ha invertido el propósito de lo que Dios le confió y se ha vuelto el rico, con su rebaño como Lázaro a la puerta. 1 Juan 3:17 pregunta cómo mora el amor de Dios en quien cierra su corazón al hermano necesitado. Que el propio nivel de vida del pastor predique contentamiento y generosidad.

sa.prompt: 28. Why does the unit say a poor man can love money as idolatrously as a rich one?
sa.model: The unit stresses that it is not money but the love of money that is the danger, and a poor man can love money as idolatrously as a rich one. The verse is constantly misquoted: it is the grip of the thing on the heart, not the thing in the hand, that condemns. The question is never how much a man has, but whom he serves. So the warning falls on rich and poor alike, wherever the heart has made money its master.

es_reference.prompt: 28. ¿Por qué dice la unidad que un pobre puede amar el dinero tan idolátricamente como un rico?
es_reference.model: La unidad subraya que el peligro no es el dinero sino el amor al dinero, y un pobre puede amar el dinero tan idolátricamente como un rico. El versículo se cita mal constantemente: lo que condena es el dominio de la cosa sobre el corazón, no la cosa en la mano. La cuestión nunca es cuánto tiene un hombre, sino a quién sirve. Así la advertencia cae igualmente sobre ricos y pobres, dondequiera que el corazón haya hecho del dinero su amo.

sa.prompt: 29. Explain the warning of the rich man and Lazarus for a comfortable church.
sa.model: In Luke 16 the rich man's sin was not that he actively robbed Lazarus but that he stepped over him day after day and did nothing, feasting while a fellow image-bearer starved at his gate. That is a sin a comfortable church commits constantly, and the Lord shows that it damns. The warning presses the church not toward careless sentimentality but toward wise, personal, dignifying love. The poor man at the door bears God's image as fully as we do.

es_reference.prompt: 29. Explique la advertencia del rico y Lázaro para una iglesia cómoda.
es_reference.model: En Lucas 16 el pecado del rico no fue que dañara activamente a Lázaro, sino que pasaba por encima de él día tras día y no hacía nada, festejando mientras un prójimo portador de la imagen de Dios moría de hambre a su puerta. Ese es un pecado que una iglesia cómoda comete constantemente, y el Señor muestra que condena. La advertencia empuja a la iglesia no a una sentimentalidad descuidada, sino a un amor sabio, personal y digno. El pobre a la puerta lleva la imagen de Dios tan plenamente como nosotros.

sa.prompt: 30. How should contentment shape the way a believer handles money day to day?
sa.model: Contentment is the great weapon against money's mastery: the contented man is free because there is nothing money can promise that he is desperate to buy. That freedom lets him work honestly, handle debt with sober care rather than presumption, save with prudence, and give with joy—to use money rather than be used by it. Teach a people contentment and you arm them against ten thousand financial follies. Leave them discontented and no income will ever be enough.

es_reference.prompt: 30. ¿Cómo debe el contentamiento moldear la manera en que un creyente maneja el dinero día a día?
es_reference.model: El contentamiento es la gran arma contra el dominio del dinero: el hombre contento es libre porque no hay nada que el dinero pueda prometerle que esté desesperado por comprar. Esa libertad lo deja trabajar honradamente, manejar la deuda con cuidado sobrio en vez de presunción, ahorrar con prudencia y dar con gozo — usar el dinero en vez de ser usado por él. Enseña al pueblo el contentamiento y lo armarás contra diez mil necedades financieras. Déjalo descontento y ningún ingreso le bastará jamás.

title: Unit 9 - Money, Stewardship, and the Poor
